8e80175cb306.Virtual appliance: A virtual appliance next hop sends traffic to a network virtual appliance (NVA) such as a firewall VM for inspection, not straight out to the internet as this question requires.
8e80175cb306.Virtual network: The Virtual network next hop keeps traffic inside the virtual network address space; it cannot be used to send matching traffic directly to the internet.
8e80175cb306.Virtual network gateway: A virtual network gateway next hop sends traffic to a VPN or ExpressRoute gateway, typically toward on-premises networks, rather than directly out to the internet.

130418afdf41.Because IP forwarding reduces latency fo: IP forwarding does not make traffic faster. It only lets the network interface accept and pass on packets addressed to other destinations, which is what a routing appliance needs.
130418afdf41.Because IP forwarding is required to ena: IP forwarding has nothing to do with encryption. Network interface encryption is not controlled by this setting; it only allows the VM to forward packets not destined for its own IP address.
130418afdf41.Because IP forwarding automatically sync: IP forwarding does not synchronize routes between virtual networks (VNets). Route propagation is handled by gateways, peering, or Azure Route Server, not by a per-interface forwarding setting.

3ab04b370c17.Virtual network: The Virtual network next hop routes traffic within the virtual network's own address space, so it cannot direct traffic to an on-premises network through a VPN gateway.
3ab04b370c17.Internet: The Internet next hop sends traffic out to the public internet, not through the VPN tunnel to the on-premises network described in this scenario.
3ab04b370c17.None: A next hop of None drops matching traffic entirely, so packets would never reach the on-premises network through the VPN gateway.

49decaca346b.It is used for routing traffic within th: A Virtual network next hop is not limited to a single subnet; it applies to the address prefix you specify within the virtual network, which can span multiple subnets.
49decaca346b.It routes traffic to a different virtual: Routing to a different virtual network is done through peering or a gateway, not a Virtual network next hop, which keeps traffic within the local virtual network's address space.
User-defined routes apply to outbound traffic leaving a subnet, not only inbound traffic, so describing this route as inbound-only misrepresents how route tables work.

Load balancing between VMs is done by Azure Load Balancer or Application Gateway. User-defined routes control traffic paths but do not distribute traffic across instances.
218caecd303e.To automatically scale out VMs based on: Automatic scale-out is handled by virtual machine scale sets and autoscale rules, not by user-defined routes, which only control where network traffic is sent.
218caecd303e.To increase the number of NSG rules beyo: User-defined routes have no effect on network security group (NSG) rule limits. NSG limits are a separate quota and routing does not change them.

f034063537d6.Budgets are automatically converted to u: Budgets are never automatically converted between cost-based and usage-based types. Exceeding a budget only triggers alerts; the budget definition stays the same.
f034063537d6.Budget alerts are created only when usin: Budget alerts can be created in the Azure portal as well. Only usage-based budget alerts are limited to the Azure Consumption API, so saying all budget alerts require the API is wrong.
f034063537d6.You cannot specify email recipients for: Budgets let you specify email recipients for alerts, along with action groups, so the claim that recipients cannot be set is false.

dd9f1bfb15a1.Azure automatically stops resource deplo: Budgets do not stop deployments or resources. Reaching a threshold only sends notifications, though you can optionally trigger automation through action groups yourself.
dd9f1bfb15a1.Azure applies a policy to block the reso: Budgets do not apply Azure Policy or lock resource groups. They monitor spending and send alerts when thresholds are reached.
dd9f1bfb15a1.Nothing happens; budgets are information: Budgets are not silent. When a threshold is reached, Azure sends a budget alert to the configured recipients, which is the main point of creating one.

9a66a7d67483.Enterprise Agreement (EA) subscription o: Cost-based budget alerts are not limited to Enterprise Agreement (EA) subscriptions; Microsoft Customer Agreement accounts support them too, so this option is too narrow.
9a66a7d67483.Azure sponsorship subscription only: Budget alerts are not restricted to sponsorship subscriptions. Support covers Microsoft Customer Agreement and Enterprise Agreement accounts broadly, apart from credit and department quota accounts.
9a66a7d67483.Visual Studio (MSDN) subscription only: Budget alerts are not limited to Visual Studio subscriptions. The documented support covers Microsoft Customer Agreement and Enterprise Agreement accounts, so this choice is far too narrow.

55dc7335b834.Only through the Azure portal: The Azure portal supports cost-based budgets; usage-based budget alerts are available only through the Azure Consumption API, so the portal is not where you get them.
55dc7335b834.Only by enabling Azure Advisor: Azure Advisor gives recommendations on cost, security, and performance. It does not create or deliver usage-based budget alerts, which come only through the Azure Consumption API.
55dc7335b834.Usage-based budgets are not supported: Usage-based budgets are supported; they just cannot be managed in the portal and must be used through the Azure Consumption API.

5eba611dc83e.Budget alerts: Budget alerts are a supported Cost Management alert type that fires when spending reaches a budget threshold, so this is not the unsupported option the question is looking for.
5eba611dc83e.Credit alerts: Credit alerts are a supported Cost Management alert type that notifies you when Azure Prepayment credits are being consumed, so they are not the unsupported option.
5eba611dc83e.Department spending quota alerts: Department spending quota alerts are supported for Enterprise Agreement departments when spending reaches a quota threshold, so they are a real Cost Management alert type.

519b18fe20b7.No, budget alerts can only be sent to te: Budget alerts are not limited to tenant administrators. You can add any email address, including addresses outside your organization.
519b18fe20b7.No, budget alerts cannot be sent to emai: Budget alerts are delivered by email to the recipients you configure, so saying they cannot be sent to email addresses is false.
519b18fe20b7.Only Azure Support can receive budget al: Budget alerts go to whatever recipients you configure, not to Azure Support. Microsoft support staff have no role in receiving your budget notifications.

ecfaba106b47.Budget alerts automatically enforce spen: Budget alerts only notify; they never stop resources or enforce spending limits on their own. Any automated response must be built separately, for example with action groups.
ecfaba106b47.Budget alerts can only be configured at: Budgets can be scoped at several levels, including subscriptions, resource groups, management groups, and billing scopes, not only resource groups.
ecfaba106b47.Budget alerts are automatically created: Budget alerts are not created automatically. You must define a budget with thresholds and recipients before any alert is sent.

58919e30200d.Budget alert: A budget alert tracks spending against a budget you define at a scope such as a subscription, not against an Enterprise Agreement department's assigned spending quota.
58919e30200d.Credit alert: Credit alerts warn when Azure Prepayment credit balances are being consumed, not when a department reaches a percentage of its quota.
58919e30200d.Usage alert: Usage alert is not a named Cost Management alert type. The supported types are budget, credit, and department spending quota alerts.

f1d02de66648.Network security groups: Network security groups (NSGs) filter network traffic with security rules. They are not metadata for organizing resources, resource groups, and subscriptions.
f1d02de66648.Role assignments: Role assignments grant access permissions through role-based access control. They control who can do what, rather than labeling resources for logical organization.
f1d02de66648.Availability zones: Availability zones are physically separate datacenter groups in a region used for resiliency. They are not labels you attach to organize resources.

ecc15b204fe3.Tag names are case‑sensitive and tag val: This reverses the actual behavior. Tag names are case-insensitive for operations, while tag values are case-sensitive.
ecc15b204fe3.Both tag names and values are case‑sensi: Tag names are not case-sensitive for operations; Azure retrieves or updates a tag regardless of the name's casing. Only tag values are case-sensitive.
ecc15b204fe3.Both tag names and values are case‑insen: Tag values are case-sensitive, so treating both names and values as case-insensitive could cause mismatched values in reports and policies.

acd30c5db4d1.Resource: Tags can be applied directly to individual resources, which is their most common use, so this is not a place where tags are unavailable.
acd30c5db4d1.Resource group: Resource groups support tags, which are often used to label environments or cost centers, so this is not the unsupported location.
acd30c5db4d1.Subscription: Subscriptions support tags, so this is not the unsupported location. Management groups are the scope where tags cannot be applied.

52f49e08d93d.Use sensitive information such as passwo: Tags are stored in plain text and readable by anyone with read access, so putting passwords or keys in them is a security risk, not a best practice.
52f49e08d93d.Apply the same tag key multiple times on: A resource cannot have duplicate tag keys; each key is unique per resource. Repeating a key is not possible and would not help cost reporting anyway.
52f49e08d93d.Create one tag with very long values to: Tag values have length limits, and packing everything into one long value makes filtering and cost reporting harder. Separate, consistent key-value pairs work better.

ae872a51bbda.Owner: Owner grants full control, including managing access, which is far broader than needed just to apply tags.
ae872a51bbda.Contributor: Contributor lets you create and manage resources, which is broader than necessary when the only goal is managing tags.
ae872a51bbda.Reader: Reader grants view-only access and cannot write tags, so it is not enough to apply tags to a resource.

2197efa5a277.Yes, tags are automatically inherited by: Resources do not automatically inherit tags from their resource group. You need Azure Policy, such as an inherit-tag policy, or automation to copy them.
2197efa5a277.Yes, but only if the resource is created: Deploying with Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates does not cause automatic inheritance. The template must set the tags explicitly, or a policy must apply them.
2197efa5a277.Only if the resource resides in the same: A resource's region has no effect on tag inheritance. Tags are never inherited automatically, whatever region the resource and resource group are in.

dc3c5985759c.Because tags are automatically encrypted: Tags are not encrypted in a special way that hides them. The concern is the opposite: tag values are plain text and visible to anyone with read access.
dc3c5985759c.Because tags reduce performance when sto: Tags have no meaningful performance impact. The reason to avoid secrets in tags is that values are visible in plain text to readers and in cost reports.
Case-insensitive tag names are unrelated to security. The real issue is that tag values are stored in plain text and readable by anyone with read access.

19a001a04fac.A resource can belong to multiple resour: A resource cannot belong to more than one resource group at the same time; it must belong to exactly one.
19a001a04fac.A resource group can contain resources f: A resource group exists within a single subscription and holds only resources from that subscription.
19a001a04fac.A resource can be unassigned to any reso: Every Azure resource must belong to a resource group. There is no option to leave a resource unassigned.

8422b2f633ec.All resources must be in the same region: Resources do not have to be in the resource group's region. A resource group can hold resources from many regions; its location only stores metadata.
The resource group location matters because it is where the group's metadata is stored, which can affect compliance and availability of management operations.
8422b2f633ec.Only storage resources must be in the sa: No resource type, including storage, is required to share the resource group's region. Resources in a group can be deployed to any supported region.

Deleting a resource group also deletes every resource in it. Resources are not left unaffected, which is why deletion should be done carefully.
f537afc8de8d.They are moved to the root of the subscr: There is no subscription root where orphaned resources go. Every resource needs a resource group, and deleting the group deletes its resources.
f537afc8de8d.They are hidden but continue to consume: Resources are not hidden while still running. Deleting the resource group deletes the resources, so they stop consuming and being billed for compute.

6eb920069b7e.Place all resources in a single resource: Putting everything in one resource group makes it hard to manage access, costs, and lifecycles separately, which goes against recommended practice.
Region alone is a weak grouping basis, since resources in one region may have unrelated lifecycles. Grouping by shared lifecycle and management needs is recommended.
6eb920069b7e.Group resources based on their SKU or pe: SKU or performance tier says nothing about how resources are managed or retired together, so it is not a recommended way to organize resource groups.

806056a6dddd.Resources can never be moved once create: Many resource types can be moved between resource groups after creation, so saying resources can never be moved is incorrect.
806056a6dddd.Resources can be moved only within the s: Resources can also be moved to a resource group in a different subscription, subject to resource-specific limitations, so moves are not limited to one subscription.
806056a6dddd.Moving resources requires redeployment v: Moving a resource is a built-in Azure Resource Manager operation through the portal, CLI, or API. It does not require redeploying from templates.

e33ad0716755.Unlimited instances: Resource groups are not unlimited. Azure limits each resource type to 800 instances per resource group by default, with some exceptions.
e33ad0716755.One instance per resource group: A resource group can hold many instances of the same resource type, up to 800 by default, not just one.
e33ad0716755.50 instances: The documented default limit is 800 instances of a resource type per resource group, not 50.

a5a2bb09a89b.It determines where the resources in the: The resource group location does not restrict where its resources are deployed. Resources can be in other regions; the location only governs where group metadata is stored.
a5a2bb09a89b.It is required only for compliance purpo: The location is not just a compliance setting. It is required and determines where the group's metadata is stored and where deployment operations are handled.
a5a2bb09a89b.It can be omitted and will default to th: The location is a required property when you create a resource group and cannot be omitted. Subscriptions have no default region to fall back on.

4e1608c5be36.Both operations succeed, and the resourc: Azure Resource Manager does not merge concurrent changes to a resource group. Conflicting operations are serialized and one is rejected with a conflict error.
4e1608c5be36.Both operations are aborted and rolled b: Both operations are not rolled back. Resource Manager lets one proceed and returns a 409 conflict to the other.
4e1608c5be36.Azure automatically resolves conflicts b: Resource Manager does not pick a winner based on timing. One operation proceeds and the other gets a 409 conflict, which the caller must retry.

12bdc36af4fc.Availability sets: Availability sets spread VMs across fault and update domains for high availability, but they do not automatically add or remove VM instances based on load.
12bdc36af4fc.Reserved VM instances: Reserved VM instances are a billing discount for committing to one or three years of compute. They provide no scaling or availability features.
12bdc36af4fc.Application security groups: Application security groups group VM network interfaces for network security group rules. They are a security feature, not a scaling mechanism.

f49135985427.Up to 100 instances: Up to 100 instances is the limit for a Uniform scale set with a custom image or single placement group, not for Flexible orchestration, which supports up to 1,000.
f49135985427.Up to 500 instances: There is no documented 500-instance limit for scale sets. Flexible orchestration mode supports up to 1,000 instances.
f49135985427.Up to 2,000 instances: Scale sets in Flexible orchestration mode support up to 1,000 instances, not 2,000, so this figure is too high.

4692d6ea9c28.Automatic scaling based on demand: Automatic scaling based on demand is a core scale set benefit, using autoscale rules or schedules, so it is not the option that fails to describe a benefit.
4692d6ea9c28.Health monitoring and automatic replacem: Scale sets do offer health monitoring and automatic instance repair to replace unhealthy VMs, so this is a genuine benefit rather than the answer.
4692d6ea9c28.Ability to deploy workloads across fault: Scale sets spread instances across fault domains and update domains, or across availability zones, to improve resilience, so this is a real benefit.

98e421c489db.A grouping of VMs across availability zo: Availability zones are separate datacenter groups within a region. A fault domain is a smaller grouping of shared hardware such as racks, power, and network switches.
98e421c489db.A network security isolation boundary: A fault domain is about physical hardware failure isolation, not network security. Network isolation comes from virtual networks, subnets, and network security groups.
98e421c489db.A region boundary that determines where: Regions decide where data resides, but a fault domain is a much smaller unit inside a datacenter that separates VMs onto different hardware.

3c6dac6a086c.A region in which VMs are deployed: A region is a geographic area containing datacenters. An update domain is a logical group of VMs that are updated or rebooted together during maintenance.
3c6dac6a086c.A domain name used to access the VMs: An update domain is not a DNS name. It is a logical grouping that controls which VMs are rebooted together during planned maintenance.
3c6dac6a086c.A classification of VMs by their operati: Update domains do not classify VMs by operating system. They group VMs so maintenance and updates are rolled out to one group at a time.

b9edf66985de.Flexible mode automatically scales based: Neither orchestration mode is tied to a specific scaling metric. Both can autoscale on CPU, network, or custom metrics; the real difference is instance uniformity and flexibility.
b9edf66985de.Flexible mode is deprecated; only unifor: Flexible orchestration is not deprecated. It is the recommended mode for most new scale set deployments, and Uniform mode remains supported too.
b9edf66985de.Uniform mode supports mixed operating sy: This reverses the modes. Uniform uses identical instances from one VM model, while Flexible is the mode that allows mixing VM sizes and configurations.

9d1286c116cc.Azure chooses the zone randomly for each: Azure does not place instances in random zones. You choose the zone or zones at deployment, and the scale set balances instances across the zones you specify.
9d1286c116cc.Scale sets cannot be deployed across zon: Scale sets can be deployed across availability zones, which is a key way to make them resilient to a zone failure.
9d1286c116cc.VMs are always placed in zone 1 unless c: There is no default of zone 1. A scale set uses the zones you specify, or none if you choose a regional deployment.

72351c8f5fba.Integration with Azure Load Balancer or: Scale sets integrate with Azure Load Balancer and Application Gateway to distribute traffic across instances, so this is a real capability rather than the answer.
72351c8f5fba.Support for spot virtual machines: Scale sets support Azure Spot Virtual Machines for discounted, interruptible capacity, so this is a genuine capability and not the answer.
72351c8f5fba.Support for auto‑healing and health prob: Scale sets support health probes and automatic instance repair to replace unhealthy VMs, so this is a real capability, not the answer.

67b45ae51f82.You are charged a separate fee for the s: There is no separate charge for the scale set object. You pay only for the VMs, disks, networking, and other resources the instances use.
67b45ae51f82.Scale sets are free but require a premiu: Scale sets need no premium subscription and are not free of resource costs. The scale set itself is free, but you pay for the resources the VMs consume.
67b45ae51f82.There is a flat monthly fee regardless o: There is no flat monthly fee. Cost depends on how many instances run and the compute, storage, and network resources they consume.

c610e880e688.A separate subscription that provides de: Availability zones are not subscriptions and do not mean dedicated hardware. Dedicated physical servers are offered by Azure Dedicated Host, a separate service.
c610e880e688.A logical grouping of virtual machines a: Logical groupings of resources are handled by resource groups or tags. An availability zone is a physical location with independent power, cooling, and networking.
c610e880e688.A region where resources can be deployed: A region is the larger geographic area that contains availability zones. A zone is one physically separate set of datacenters inside a region.

546392121145.One zone: A single zone would provide no zone redundancy. Azure regions that support availability zones have at least three zones.
546392121145.Two zones: Two zones is not the standard configuration. Zone-enabled Azure regions have a minimum of three availability zones.
546392121145.Five zones: Five zones is not typical. Azure regions that support availability zones normally have three.

4beb2451df04.10–50 milliseconds: Ten to fifty milliseconds is more typical of traffic between regions. Azure targets round-trip latency under 2 milliseconds between zones in the same region.
4beb2451df04.100 milliseconds: One hundred milliseconds is far too high for zones within a region, which are designed for under 2 milliseconds of round-trip latency.
4beb2451df04.1 second: A full second of latency would make synchronous replication impossible. Availability zones in a region are designed for under 2 milliseconds of round-trip latency.

a96b7c04ddc7.Zonal deployments: Zonal deployments pin a resource to one specific zone, so they do not replicate across zones or fail over automatically if that zone goes down.
a96b7c04ddc7.Non‑zonal (regional) deployments: Non-zonal (regional) deployments do not specify a zone and offer no guaranteed protection or automatic failover if a zone fails.
a96b7c04ddc7.Single instance deployments: A single instance deployment lives in one place, with no replication across zones and no automatic failover.

fe8fc04b1120.Zone‑redundant deployment: Zone-redundant deployments spread or replicate a resource across multiple zones rather than pinning it to one specific zone.
fe8fc04b1120.Regional deployment: A regional (non-zonal) deployment lets Azure place the resource anywhere in the region without a zone guarantee, so it does not pin it to a specific zone.
fe8fc04b1120.Geo‑redundant deployment: Geo-redundant deployments replicate data to a secondary region. They protect against regional outages and do not pin a resource to a specific zone.

e791ab13019f.They are not recommended because they pr: Non-zonal deployments are still a valid choice for some workloads. The issue is lack of zone resilience, not that they are always discouraged or have no redundancy at all.
e791ab13019f.They distribute resources across multipl: Spreading resources across multiple zones describes zone-redundant deployments. Non-zonal deployments specify no zone and get no automatic zone distribution.
e791ab13019f.They are only available in preview regio: Non-zonal deployments are the default option in all regions, not a preview-only feature.

39383065f805.All customers see the same physical mapp: Physical zone mapping is not the same for every customer. Logical zone numbers are mapped to physical zones per subscription and can differ.
39383065f805.Zones are always mapped to specific data: Zones are not tied to fixed, identical locations across subscriptions. Logical zone numbers can map to different physical datacenters in each subscription.
39383065f805.Zone mapping refers to the DNS zone used: Zone mapping has nothing to do with Azure DNS zones. It refers to how logical availability zone numbers map to physical zones in a region.

09b148c7e3f5.Deploy all components in a single zone a: Putting every component in one zone makes that zone a single point of failure. Cross-region replication helps with regional disasters but does not replace zone redundancy.
09b148c7e3f5.Deploy resources across zones and disabl: Spreading resources across zones without load balancing leaves traffic unable to shift away from a failed zone, which defeats the purpose of zone redundancy.
09b148c7e3f5.Deploy resources only in the primary zon: Running only in a primary zone with manual failover means downtime during a zone outage. Recommended designs spread layers across zones for automatic resilience.

8ce9878d9420.Yes, there is a cost for data transferre: Microsoft has stopped charging for data transfer between availability zones in the same region, so saying there is a cost is outdated.
8ce9878d9420.Yes, but only for Standard storage accou: Inter-zone data transfer is not billed for any storage tier, Standard or otherwise, so tying a charge to Standard storage accounts is wrong.
The removal of inter-zone data transfer charges applies across services, so the answer does not depend on which service you use.

a8abb00e6bc5.Load Balancer: Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4 on TCP and UDP traffic and cannot inspect URL paths or host headers.
a8abb00e6bc5.Traffic Manager: Traffic Manager is a DNS-based global traffic router. It returns endpoint addresses in DNS responses and never inspects HTTP requests, so it cannot route on URL path or host header.
a8abb00e6bc5.Azure DNS: Azure DNS hosts DNS zones and resolves names. It does not load balance HTTP traffic or make decisions based on URL paths or host headers.

c8ba4fc44eb6.Azure Load Balancer operates at OSI laye: This reverses the layers. Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4 (TCP/UDP), while Application Gateway works at layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS).
c8ba4fc44eb6.Azure Load Balancer includes a Web Appli: Web Application Firewall (WAF) is offered on Application Gateway, not Azure Load Balancer, so this statement gets the feature backwards.
c8ba4fc44eb6.Application Gateway is used only for out: Application Gateway mainly handles inbound web traffic to backend applications. Outbound connectivity is typically provided by Load Balancer outbound rules or NAT Gateway.

c107729b0a65.Azure Load Balancer: Azure Load Balancer is a layer 4 TCP/UDP service with no Web Application Firewall (WAF) capability, so it cannot inspect HTTP requests for web attacks.
c107729b0a65.Traffic Manager: Traffic Manager routes traffic using DNS and never sees HTTP requests, so it cannot provide Web Application Firewall (WAF) protection.
c107729b0a65.Azure DNS: Azure DNS only resolves domain names. It does not load balance traffic or offer any Web Application Firewall (WAF) functionality.

f699a2bfa11b.Azure Load Balancer: Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4 and cannot see HTTP URL paths, so it cannot send /images and /video requests to different backends.
f699a2bfa11b.Traffic Manager: Traffic Manager is DNS-based and only chooses an endpoint at name-resolution time. It never sees the URL path, so it cannot do path-based routing.
f699a2bfa11b.Azure DNS: Azure DNS resolves domain names to addresses and has no view of HTTP request paths, so it cannot route requests based on the URL.

68ad7e66ae63.Azure Load Balancer: Azure Load Balancer is a layer 4 service, so it cannot terminate SSL/TLS or use cookie-based session affinity, which requires HTTP awareness.
68ad7e66ae63.Traffic Manager: Traffic Manager works only at the DNS level and never handles the client connection, so it cannot terminate SSL or set affinity cookies.
68ad7e66ae63.Azure DNS: Azure DNS only resolves names and does not proxy traffic, so it offers neither SSL termination nor cookie-based session affinity.

a7d0dee44fc2.It provides layer 7 load balancing for H: Traffic Manager is not a layer 7 regional load balancer. That describes Application Gateway; Traffic Manager routes globally using DNS.
a7d0dee44fc2.It performs SSL termination like Applica: Traffic Manager never terminates SSL, because clients connect directly to the endpoint after DNS resolution. SSL termination is done by Application Gateway or Front Door.
a7d0dee44fc2.It automatically blocks traffic from unt: Traffic Manager has no built-in IP blocking. Filtering untrusted traffic is done with network security groups, Azure Firewall, or a Web Application Firewall (WAF).

84d937f1c110.Azure Load Balancer: Azure Load Balancer distributes traffic within a region at layer 4 and does not choose between global endpoints by performance or location.
84d937f1c110.Application Gateway: Application Gateway is a regional layer 7 load balancer, so it does not route users to the best global endpoint across regions.
84d937f1c110.Azure Front Door Service: Front Door also routes users globally, but it is a layer 7 HTTP/HTTPS edge service. The DNS-based choice of the best global endpoint by performance or geography is what Traffic Manager provides.

daa6872a6927.Azure DNS: Azure DNS hosts domains and resolves names. It offers no HTTP acceleration, caching, or advanced layer 7 routing at global entry points.
daa6872a6927.Traffic Manager: Traffic Manager uses DNS to point clients to endpoints but does not proxy traffic, so it offers no acceleration, caching, or edge Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) protection.
daa6872a6927.Application Gateway: Application Gateway is a regional layer 7 load balancer, not a global edge entry point with caching and acceleration.

ab99cfccbb12.Load balancing non‑HTTP traffic across v: Application Gateway handles only HTTP/HTTPS traffic, so non-HTTP workloads are better suited to Azure Load Balancer.
ab99cfccbb12.Providing DNS‑based routing across regio: DNS-based routing across regions for any protocol describes Traffic Manager, not Application Gateway, which is a regional HTTP/HTTPS load balancer.
ab99cfccbb12.Routing UDP packets between IoT devices: Application Gateway does not handle UDP. UDP traffic needs Azure Load Balancer, which works at layer 4.

520d235465b7.It operates at the application layer (HT: Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4 (TCP/UDP), not the application layer. HTTP/HTTPS-aware balancing is provided by Application Gateway or Front Door.
Azure Load Balancer passes traffic through without decrypting it, so it has no built-in SSL termination. That feature belongs to Application Gateway or Front Door.
Load Balancer comes in Standard and Gateway SKUs, and the Basic SKU has been retired, so it is not limited to Basic.

Path-based routing is a layer 7 feature of Application Gateway and Front Door. Standard Load Balancer works at layer 4 and cannot route on URL paths.
Standard Load Balancer includes no Web Application Firewall (WAF); WAF is offered with Application Gateway and Front Door, and it is unrelated to zone resiliency.
093cf3883dd9.It automatically scales based on CPU usa: Load Balancer does not scale backend VMs on CPU usage. That is the job of autoscale on virtual machine scale sets, not a load balancer feature.

72e51e5cf22a.A diagnostic tool for monitoring virtual: Network latency monitoring is done by tools like Network Watcher connection monitor. A health probe checks whether backend instances can receive traffic.
72e51e5cf22a.A method for enabling real‑time monitori: A health probe is not an Azure Monitor feature for real-time monitoring. It is used by the load balancer to decide which backend instances get traffic.
72e51e5cf22a.An alert generated when CPU usage exceed: CPU threshold alerts are created in Azure Monitor. A health probe checks a port or endpoint on each backend to determine whether that instance is healthy.

6238b8ae035e.Internal Load Balancer: An internal load balancer uses only private IP addresses inside a virtual network, so it cannot direct internet traffic to individual VMs with inbound NAT rules.
6238b8ae035e.Traffic Manager: Traffic Manager is a DNS-based router with no NAT rules, so it cannot forward internet traffic to specific VM ports.
6238b8ae035e.Application Gateway: Application Gateway is a layer 7 HTTP/HTTPS load balancer and does not offer the inbound and outbound NAT rules used to reach individual VMs.

19be146abe10.Basic Load Balancer supports only inboun: Basic Load Balancer does support inbound load balancing and default outbound access. Its weaknesses are limited scale, no zone support, and no SLA, and it has been retired.
19be146abe10.Basic Load Balancer supports outbound co: This is backwards. Standard Load Balancer supports outbound connectivity with explicit outbound rules, and outbound control is one of its advantages.
19be146abe10.Standard Load Balancer is free of charge: Standard Load Balancer is billed by rules and data processed, so it is not free. It is recommended for its features and SLA, not its price.

b0aa77ce40b3.It opens all ports to the internet by de: Load Balancer does not open all ports to the internet. Standard Load Balancer is secure by default, and traffic must be allowed by network security groups and rules.
SSL offloading decrypts HTTPS traffic at a layer 7 proxy such as Application Gateway. Load Balancer does not decrypt traffic and handles outbound connections with source NAT.
Azure DNS resolves names and does not translate addresses. Outbound connections through Load Balancer rely on source network address translation (SNAT) to its public IP.

9bcedb703c94.A private Load Balancer does not support: Internal load balancers support UDP just like public ones, since both handle TCP and UDP at layer 4.

735c6cf53e88.Geo-redundant storage (GRS): GRS keeps three copies in one datacenter in the primary region plus copies in a paired secondary region; it does not spread copies across availability zones.

503f2df7e755.Zone-redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS replicates across availability zones within a single region only; it has no secondary region and therefore no secondary read endpoint.
503f2df7e755.Geo-zone‑redundant storage (GZRS): GZRS replicates to a secondary region but, without the read-access option, the secondary copy cannot be read until a failover occurs.

eb286fd15862.Locally redundant storage (LRS): LRS keeps three copies in one datacenter only, providing neither zone redundancy nor replication to a secondary region.
eb286fd15862.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS provides zone redundancy within the primary region but does not replicate to a secondary region, so it lacks regional failover.
eb286fd15862.Geo-redundant storage (GRS): GRS replicates to a secondary region, but in the primary region it uses LRS within one datacenter rather than spreading copies across availability zones.

12968299b700.Locally redundant storage (LRS): LRS offers 11 nines of durability within a single datacenter and has no secondary region, so a regional outage leaves the data unavailable.
12968299b700.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS offers 12 nines of durability across zones in one region; it does not replicate to another region, so a full regional outage makes the data unavailable.
12968299b700.Geo‑redundant storage (GRS): GRS also reaches 16 nines of durability, but the secondary copy cannot be read until failover, so data is not available during a regional outage without that step.

b1e8bbf01343.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS spreads its three copies across separate availability zones rather than one datacenter, and it provides 12 nines of durability rather than 11.
b1e8bbf01343.Geo‑redundant storage (GRS): GRS keeps three local copies in the primary region but also replicates to a secondary region for a total of six copies and 16 nines of durability.
b1e8bbf01343.Geo‑zone‑redundant storage (GZRS): GZRS replicates across three availability zones and to a secondary region, so it does not keep its copies within a single datacenter.

4072af24eae5.Lower storage costs due to fewer copies: ZRS keeps the same number of copies as LRS (three) and costs more, not less, because it spreads them across availability zones.
4072af24eae5.Replication to a secondary region: ZRS does not replicate to a secondary region; cross-region replication comes from GRS or GZRS, not from choosing ZRS over LRS.
4072af24eae5.Read access to replicated data in a seco: Read access to a secondary region is provided by RA-GRS or RA-GZRS; ZRS stays within one region and has no secondary read endpoint.

8173783f7ead.To reduce storage costs while maintainin: GRS does not provide zone isolation; its primary-region copies sit in one datacenter. Its value is cross-region protection, not cheaper zone redundancy.
8173783f7ead.To improve performance by replicating ac: Replicating across availability zones is what ZRS does; GRS does not use zones in the primary region and does not improve performance.
8173783f7ead.Because ZRS only supports block blobs: This is not true; ZRS supports blobs, files, queues and tables in general-purpose v2 accounts, so service support is not a reason to pick GRS.

d6934dc96f2e.Locally redundant storage (LRS): LRS keeps copies only in one datacenter of the primary region, so there is no secondary region to read from when the primary is down.
d6934dc96f2e.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS replicates only across zones within the primary region; if the whole region is unavailable, there is no secondary endpoint to read from.
d6934dc96f2e.Geo‑redundant storage (GRS): GRS does replicate to a secondary region, but that copy is not readable until a failover occurs, so it provides no secondary read endpoint.

6f837e4bf8d1.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS replicates synchronously across zones but never to another region, so it lacks the asynchronous cross-region replication the question describes.
6f837e4bf8d1.Geo‑redundant storage (GRS): GRS replicates asynchronously to a secondary region, but within the primary region it uses LRS in one datacenter, not synchronous replication across zones.
6f837e4bf8d1.Read‑access geo‑zone‑redundant storage (: RA-GZRS has the same replication pattern but adds a read-only secondary endpoint, which the question explicitly excludes.

a1f4b751ee71.Locally redundant storage (LRS): LRS writes all three copies synchronously before acknowledging a write, so it has no asynchronous replication lag to cause data loss.
a1f4b751ee71.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS replicates synchronously across three availability zones, so a write is not acknowledged until all copies are stored, avoiding asynchronous replication loss.
a1f4b751ee71.Read‑access geo‑zone‑redundant storage (: RA-GZRS replicates synchronously across zones in the primary region, but note its copy to the secondary region is also asynchronous; the question focuses on GRS as the classic asynchronous example.

099df5f85d77.Locally redundant storage (LRS): LRS keeps all copies in one datacenter, so a datacenter outage can make data unavailable; it does not meet the availability requirement.
099df5f85d77.Geo‑redundant storage (GRS): GRS adds protection against regional disasters, which the scenario does not need, and its primary copies sit in a single datacenter rather than across zones.
099df5f85d77.Read‑access geo‑redundant storage (RA‑GR: RA-GRS adds a readable secondary region for regional disasters, which is unnecessary cost here, and it does not spread primary copies across zones.

b37bdb24db20.Locally redundant storage (LRS): LRS keeps data in a single datacenter in one region, so it meets neither the multi-region nor the zone redundancy requirement.
b37bdb24db20.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS provides zone redundancy in the primary region but does not replicate to any other region, so the multi-region requirement is not met.
b37bdb24db20.Geo‑redundant storage (GRS): GRS replicates to a secondary region, but its primary-region copies are in one datacenter rather than across availability zones.

7ed7c8115e85.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS spreads copies across three availability zones, which costs more than LRS; it suits higher availability needs rather than the cheapest option.
7ed7c8115e85.Geo‑redundant storage (GRS): GRS adds a second region with three more copies, so it costs more than LRS and exceeds moderate durability requirements for a regional app.
7ed7c8115e85.Geo‑zone‑redundant storage (GZRS): GZRS combines zone and cross-region replication, making it one of the most expensive options and unnecessary for moderate durability needs.

339f731936b0.Locally redundant storage (LRS): LRS has no secondary region at all, so during a region-wide outage there is nowhere else to read the data from.
339f731936b0.Geo‑redundant storage (GRS): GRS replicates to a secondary region, but you cannot read that copy until a failover completes, so reads cannot switch immediately.
339f731936b0.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS replicates only within the primary region, so a region-wide outage takes down all zones' access and there is no other region to read from.

d81e9e120578.Read‑access geo‑redundant storage (RA‑GR: RA-GRS exposes a read-only secondary endpoint at all times, so it supports serving read traffic from the secondary region during normal operations.
d81e9e120578.Read‑access geo‑zone‑redundant storage (: RA-GZRS adds a readable secondary endpoint to GZRS, so it is a suitable choice for serving reads from the secondary region, not one to avoid.
d81e9e120578.Geo‑zone‑redundant storage (GZRS): GZRS also lacks a readable secondary, so it would be unsuitable too; however, the question targets GRS as the standard example without read access.

b68d64748ade.Locally redundant storage (LRS): LRS keeps three synchronous copies, but all in one datacenter, and has no secondary region, so cross-region reads are impossible.
b68d64748ade.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS keeps three synchronous copies across zones but does not replicate to another region, so it cannot provide reads from a second region.
b68d64748ade.Geo‑redundant storage (GRS): GRS replicates to another region but its secondary copy is not readable before failover, and primary copies are not spread across zones.

d1a64689c8ad.Read‑access geo‑redundant storage (RA‑GR: RA-GRS adds read access to the secondary region, which the scenario explicitly does not need, so it costs more than necessary.
d1a64689c8ad.Read‑access geo‑zone‑redundant storage (: RA-GZRS adds zone redundancy and secondary read access, neither of which the scenario requires, making it a more expensive choice than needed.
d1a64689c8ad.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS does not replicate to another region, so it offers no protection against data loss during a region failover.

1b4625f015df.Locally redundant storage (LRS): LRS keeps data in one datacenter, so it protects against neither zone-level nor region-level failures and has no secondary read access.
1b4625f015df.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS protects against zone failures but has no secondary region, so it cannot survive a regional outage or support reporting reads from another region.
1b4625f015df.Read‑access geo‑redundant storage (RA‑GR: RA-GRS provides secondary-region reads, but its primary copies are in one datacenter rather than across zones, so it lacks zone-level protection.

dc8aa772f333.Locally redundant storage (LRS): LRS keeps copies in one datacenter and does not use three zones or a secondary region, so it offers no regional failover at all.
dc8aa772f333.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS replicates across three zones but never to another region, so there is no regional failover target and no cross-region recovery point.
dc8aa772f333.Geo‑redundant storage (GRS): GRS replicates to a secondary region but its primary copies are not spread across three zones, so it fails the zone requirement.

9c6fadc91bd6.Because ZRS replicates data to a seconda: ZRS does not replicate to a secondary region; it stays within one region, so global availability is not its purpose.
9c6fadc91bd6.Because ZRS is the only option that supp: ZRS is not a cross-region option at all, and no redundancy choice exists specifically to satisfy cross-region compliance this way.
9c6fadc91bd6.Because ZRS stores fewer copies to save: ZRS keeps three copies, the same as LRS, and costs more; its advantage is spreading those copies across availability zones.

6d8b90be0c56.Geo‑redundant storage (GRS): GRS adds replication to a secondary region, which the budget does not allow, and its primary copies are not spread across zones.
6d8b90be0c56.Read‑access geo‑redundant storage (RA‑GR: RA-GRS adds a readable secondary region, the extra regional replication the budget rules out, and it lacks zone redundancy in the primary region.

81993993deb8.RA‑GZRS replicates data only to a second: This reverses the two: RA-GZRS is the one with zone replication in the primary region, while RA-GRS uses a single datacenter there.
81993993deb8.Both RA‑GRS and RA‑GZRS replicate across: Only RA-GZRS replicates across three zones in the primary region; RA-GRS keeps its primary copies in a single datacenter, though both offer secondary reads.
81993993deb8.RA‑GRS provides zone redundancy in the s: Neither option uses zone redundancy in the secondary region; both store LRS-style copies there, and only RA-GZRS uses zones in the primary region.

96aac7754309.Zone‑redundant storage (ZRS): ZRS costs more than LRS because it spreads copies across availability zones, which rarely accessed archived logs typically do not need.
96aac7754309.Read‑access geo‑redundant storage (RA‑GR: RA-GRS adds a readable secondary region, raising cost well above LRS for logs that are rarely accessed and do not need cross-region reads.
96aac7754309.Read‑access geo‑zone‑redundant storage (: RA-GZRS is among the most expensive options, combining zones, a secondary region and read access, which is excessive for archived logs.

fb39bbd5c7f7.GRS provides 9 nines of durability becau: GRS provides 16 nines of durability, not 9; asynchronous replication to a second region increases durability rather than lowering it.
fb39bbd5c7f7.RA‑GRS offers the same durability as LRS: RA-GRS keeps six copies across two regions and offers 16 nines of durability, far more than the 11 nines of LRS.

5bd41db796e6.Service SAS: A service SAS is signed with the storage account key, not Microsoft Entra credentials, so it lacks the security benefit the question describes.
5bd41db796e6.Account SAS: An account SAS is signed with the storage account key and can grant broad access across services, so it is the less secure option.
5bd41db796e6.Stored access policy: A stored access policy is not a SAS type; it is a container-level set of constraints that a service SAS can reference, and it still relies on the account key.

34de3517944a.Service SAS: A service SAS is signed with the account key but grants access to resources in only one storage service, not multiple services.
34de3517944a.User delegation SAS: A user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key obtained via Microsoft Entra ID, not the storage account key.
34de3517944a.Ad‑hoc SAS: Ad-hoc SAS just means a SAS whose constraints are in the token rather than a stored access policy; it is not a separate type spanning multiple services.

c9ad9f283308.Account SAS: An account SAS is signed with the account key, but it can grant access across multiple services in the account, not just one.
c9ad9f283308.User delegation SAS: A user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key from Microsoft Entra credentials rather than the storage account key.
c9ad9f283308.Stored access policy: A stored access policy is not a SAS type; it defines constraints that a service SAS can reference so they can be changed or revoked centrally.

102e78b4e05d.It uses the storage account key, which s: A user delegation SAS specifically avoids the storage account key; it is signed with a user delegation key obtained using Microsoft Entra credentials.
102e78b4e05d.It allows access to multiple services in: Access across multiple services at once describes an account SAS; a user delegation SAS is scoped to resources in a service.
A user delegation SAS does require role assignments; the caller needs an Azure role permitting it to obtain a user delegation key and the data actions granted.

a90261a0ef61.It encrypts the SAS token using TLS cert: Stored access policies have nothing to do with TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificates; they hold permissions and time windows, not encryption settings.
The SAS signature is still part of the token users receive; a stored access policy does not hide it, it only centralizes the constraints.
a90261a0ef61.It automatically logs all SAS operations: Stored access policies do not configure logging; SAS requests are logged through storage diagnostic settings in Azure Monitor, independently of any policy.

07a3608a991b.Because SAS tokens expire too quickly; u: Managed identities do not extend SAS lifetimes; expiry is set in the token or policy, and expiring too quickly is not why generation should be restricted.
07a3608a991b.Because SAS tokens do not work with clie: SAS tokens work alongside client-side encryption; encryption is unrelated to controlling who is allowed to generate SAS tokens.
07a3608a991b.Because SAS tokens require custom domain: SAS tokens do not require custom domains, and service endpoints restrict network access from virtual networks rather than controlling who generates a SAS.

3f44eae2d7f1.They are automatically revoked when you: Regenerating the account key used to sign an ad-hoc SAS does invalidate it, but that is a manual, disruptive action rather than a way to revoke individual tokens.
3f44eae2d7f1.They are stored by Azure and can be view: Azure does not store or track SAS tokens; they are generated client-side and cannot be viewed in the portal after creation.
3f44eae2d7f1.They support only read and write permiss: Ad-hoc SAS tokens support the full range of permissions, such as read, write, delete, list, add and create, not just read and write.

dfe684738ecc.Only for read operations from blob stora: A stored access policy can grant any supported permissions, including write, delete and list, not just reads from blob storage.
dfe684738ecc.Never; stored access policies are deprec: Stored access policies are not deprecated; they remain the recommended way to manage and revoke service SAS tokens centrally.

d71f86544d87.Blob storage: Blob storage has supported user delegation SAS from the start, and it is the main service where this Entra-based SAS is recommended.
d71f86544d87.Azure Queue storage: Queue storage now supports user delegation SAS with recent service versions, so a service SAS is no longer the only option there.
d71f86544d87.Azure Table storage: Table storage now supports user delegation SAS with recent service versions, so a service SAS is no longer the only option there.

bfcefe65a3e1.The signed expiry field: The signed expiry field (se) sets when the SAS stops being valid; it controls timing, not whether a client can read, write or list.

992a38cdc61a.The storage account must have encryption: Encryption at rest cannot be turned off for Azure Storage, and it has no bearing on whether you can create a user delegation SAS.
992a38cdc61a.The storage account must be configured i: Access tiers such as Hot, Cool and Archive affect storage pricing and latency, not the ability to request a user delegation key.
992a38cdc61a.The storage account must be restricted t: Virtual network restrictions control network access to the account; they are not a prerequisite for generating a user delegation SAS.
