a2c021906689.Service SAS: A service SAS is signed with the storage account key, so it does not avoid reliance on the key the scenario wants to protect.
a2c021906689.Stored access policy: A stored access policy is not a SAS type; it is a set of constraints referenced by a service SAS, which is still signed with the account key.

245175644cd4.Encryption is disabled by default and mu: Server-side encryption is enabled by default for every storage account and cannot be disabled, so no manual enabling is needed.
245175644cd4.Encryption is applied only to blob data,: Server-side encryption covers all storage services, including blobs, files, queues and tables, along with their metadata.
245175644cd4.Only customer‑managed keys are supported: Microsoft-managed keys are the default; customer-managed keys are optional for those who want more control over the keys.

Microsoft-managed keys are the default, but customer-managed keys in Azure Key Vault or Key Vault Managed HSM (hardware security module) are also supported.
4e97c8958710.Only customer‑managed keys stored in you: Customer-managed keys must live in Azure Key Vault or Key Vault Managed HSM, not your own datacenter, and Microsoft-managed keys are also available.
4e97c8958710.Server‑side encryption uses the credenti: Connection string credentials authorize access to the account; they are not encryption keys, and server-side encryption uses Microsoft-managed or customer-managed keys.

cdc7607cedce.You can disable encryption by editing th: No storage account setting disables server-side encryption; it is always on, and you can only choose which keys are used.
cdc7607cedce.Encryption can be turned off only for bl: Encryption applies to all data in the account, and it cannot be turned off for blob containers or any other service.
cdc7607cedce.Encryption is optional for Premium tier: Premium storage accounts are encrypted at rest just like standard accounts; encryption is mandatory for every performance tier.

17006653ef84.Azure Active Directory: Azure Active Directory, now Microsoft Entra ID, handles identity and access, not storage of encryption keys; it can authorize Key Vault access but does not hold the keys.
17006653ef84.Azure Resource Manager: Azure Resource Manager is the deployment and management layer for Azure resources; it does not store or manage encryption keys.
17006653ef84.Azure Monitor: Azure Monitor collects metrics and logs for observability; it does not store or manage customer-managed encryption keys.

4347182f32d0.CPKs are used instead of server‑side enc: Customer-provided keys are sent with each request and are not stored in Azure Key Vault; that describes customer-managed keys. CPK also adds to, rather than replaces, the built-in server-side encryption.
4347182f32d0.CPKs are required when using premium sto: Customer-provided keys are an optional feature for Blob Storage requests, not a requirement of any performance tier. Premium storage is encrypted by default with Microsoft-managed keys like every other tier.
4347182f32d0.CPKs replace the need for customer‑manag: Customer-provided keys and customer-managed keys are separate options: CPK supplies a key per request, while customer-managed keys sit in Key Vault and protect the whole account or scope. One does not make the other unnecessary.

ad98f82d29da.RSA‑2048: RSA-2048 is an asymmetric algorithm used for things like key wrapping and signatures, not for bulk encryption of stored data. Azure Storage encrypts data at rest with a symmetric block cipher.
ad98f82d29da.AES‑128: AES-128 uses a 128-bit key, but Azure Storage server-side encryption uses the stronger 256-bit key length of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) for data and metadata at rest.
ad98f82d29da.ChaCha20: ChaCha20 is a stream cipher mostly seen in Transport Layer Security (TLS) cipher suites for data in transit. Azure Storage does not use it for server-side encryption of data at rest.

1c23694c0aac.Yes, encryption increases storage transa: Server-side encryption is applied automatically to every storage write and is not billed as extra transactions. Transaction charges are the same whether or not you think about encryption.
1c23694c0aac.Yes, encryption requires a dedicated Pre: Encryption at rest is enabled on all storage accounts and all tiers, including Standard. There is no special Premium tier needed to get it.
1c23694c0aac.Yes, encryption adds network egress char: Egress charges depend on data leaving a region or Azure, not on encryption. Server-side encryption happens inside the storage service and adds no network charges.

a6d2a3463b9f.Encrypting the data manually before uplo: With customer-managed keys, Azure Storage still performs the encryption and decryption on the server side. Encrypting data yourself before upload is client-side encryption, a separate approach.
a6d2a3463b9f.Encrypting network traffic using TLS 1.3: Transport Layer Security (TLS) protects data in transit and is configured through the account's minimum TLS version, not through customer-managed keys, which only control the key used for encryption at rest.
a6d2a3463b9f.Managing firewall settings for storage a: Firewall and network rules control who can reach the storage account. They are a network access concern and have nothing to do with owning the encryption keys for data at rest.

1698a1251dba.Data is replicated without encryption an: Azure Storage never sends data unencrypted between regions for replication. Data encrypted in the primary region stays encrypted in transit and when written to the secondary region.
1698a1251dba.Only metadata is encrypted during replic: Server-side encryption covers both data and metadata, and replication to the secondary region keeps all of it encrypted. There is no mode where only metadata is protected.
1698a1251dba.Replication only occurs for unencrypted: All data in Azure Storage is encrypted at rest, so there is no unencrypted data to pick out. Geo-replication works on encrypted data and never requires decrypting blobs first.

55f619e1a3af.Data at rest encryption also encrypts da: Encryption at rest protects data stored on disk only. Data moving over the network is protected separately by HTTPS/Transport Layer Security (TLS), which you enforce with settings like secure transfer required.
55f619e1a3af.Encryption automatically compresses data: Encryption and compression are different things, and Azure Storage server-side encryption does not compress data before sending it. Encryption at rest has no effect on the transfer format.
55f619e1a3af.Data must be decrypted before leaving th: The service decrypts data transparently before returning it to an authorized client, but that is how reads work, not a protection for data in transit. TLS is what secures the data on the wire.

996975753280.Virtual network rule: Virtual network rules allow traffic from specific subnets that have a storage service endpoint. They cannot cover an Azure service that does not run in your virtual network, which is the case in this question.
996975753280.IP network rule: IP network rules allow specific public IPv4 addresses or ranges. Many Azure platform services use shared or changing addresses, so they cannot be reliably allowed with IP rules.
996975753280.Trusted Azure services rule: The trusted Azure services exception lets a fixed list of Microsoft services bypass the firewall broadly. It is a general exception, not a rule that targets one specific resource instance as this question asks.

85174286e87b.All traffic from the internet is blocked: A new storage account allows public network traffic from all networks by default. Internet traffic is blocked only after you change the default action to deny and add network rules.
85174286e87b.Traffic is allowed only from trusted Azu: Trusted Azure services is an optional exception you use once the firewall is restricting traffic. It is not the default state of a new storage account, which accepts traffic from any network.
85174286e87b.Traffic is allowed only from the virtual: By default there is no restriction to a virtual network or region. Limiting access to particular subnets needs virtual network rules, which you must add yourself.

7853f57b1d40.Virtual network rule: Virtual network rules allow traffic from specific subnets in Azure virtual networks, identified by subnet rather than by IP address. Allowing specific IP addresses or ranges is done with IP network rules.
7853f57b1d40.Resource instance rule: Resource instance rules allow specific Azure resource instances, identified by resource ID, to reach the storage account. They do not take IP addresses or ranges.
7853f57b1d40.Service endpoint rule: There is no separate service endpoint rule type. Service endpoints are a subnet setting that virtual network rules depend on, and they do not let you list IP addresses or ranges.

038e69bc7146.Up to 100: 100 is below the actual limit. A single storage account supports up to 400 virtual network rules, so 100 understates how many subnets you can allow.
038e69bc7146.Up to 200: 200 is not the documented limit. A storage account supports up to 400 virtual network rules.
038e69bc7146.Up to 1000: 1000 exceeds the documented limit. A storage account supports a maximum of 400 virtual network rules.

d4fc1e6712a1.Virtual network rule: Virtual network rules allow traffic only from specific subnets with service endpoints. Services like Azure Backup and Azure Site Recovery do not run in your subnets, so these rules would not let them in.
d4fc1e6712a1.IP network rule: IP network rules allow specific public IPv4 addresses. Azure Backup and Site Recovery do not use fixed addresses you could list, so IP rules are not the way to let them through.
d4fc1e6712a1.Resource instance rule: Resource instance rules allow named resource instances of certain services by resource ID. The built-in exception that lets services such as Azure Backup and Site Recovery bypass the firewall is the trusted services setting.

0886e1daa959.BGP peering: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) peering exchanges routes for VPN or ExpressRoute connections. It has nothing to do with letting a subnet's traffic match a storage account's virtual network rule.
0886e1daa959.VNet peering: VNet peering connects two virtual networks to each other. A storage virtual network rule instead needs the subnet to have the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint enabled.
0886e1daa959.NAT Gateway: A NAT gateway gives a subnet a shared outbound public IP address. Traffic through it would arrive as a public IP, not as subnet traffic that a virtual network rule can match.

5ba9acc8bfa2.The request is allowed but throttled to: Azure Storage firewall rules do not throttle traffic. A request that matches no allowed rule is rejected outright, not let through at a lower speed.
5ba9acc8bfa2.The request is routed through the Azure: Network rules do not reroute blocked requests through Azure Content Delivery Network (CDN). A request from an IP address that no rule allows is simply denied.
5ba9acc8bfa2.The request is automatically redirected: The storage firewall never redirects requests to another region. A request that matches no network rule is denied with an authorization error.

aaeb877754b3.Only IPv6 addresses: Storage account IP network rules are built around public IPv4 addresses and ranges. They are not limited to IPv6, so this option misstates what the rules support.
aaeb877754b3.Only private IP addresses from within Az: IP network rules cannot use private addresses from inside Azure. To allow traffic from Azure virtual networks you use virtual network rules or private endpoints instead.
aaeb877754b3.Only addresses with CIDR /32 prefix: IP network rules accept whole Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) ranges as well as single addresses. They are not limited to /32 entries, though very small prefixes such as /31 and /32 are written as individual addresses.

2da4e8fb0835.It removes the need for network security: Network security groups filter traffic in a virtual network and still matter with identity-based authentication. Kerberos sign-in changes who is authenticated, not what network controls you need.
2da4e8fb0835.It encrypts files using client‑side encr: Identity-based authentication is about verifying users with Kerberos, not encrypting files on the client. Data is still encrypted at rest by the service, and client-side encryption is a separate concept.
2da4e8fb0835.It automatically blocks anonymous read a: Azure Files SMB shares do not support anonymous access in the first place. The security gain from identity-based authentication is replacing a shared account key with per-user domain credentials.

e80bc5fc0144.Only Microsoft Entra ID (cloud‑only): Azure Files is not limited to Microsoft Entra ID alone. It supports three sources: on-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS), Microsoft Entra Domain Services, and Microsoft Entra Kerberos.
e80bc5fc0144.Google Workspace and LDAP: Google Workspace and generic Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) directories are not supported identity sources for Azure Files. SMB authentication relies on Kerberos from AD DS, Entra Domain Services, or Entra Kerberos.
e80bc5fc0144.Any OIDC provider: Azure Files SMB authentication uses Kerberos tickets, not OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens. Arbitrary OIDC identity providers cannot be used as an identity source for file shares.

780be327c533.You must deploy an Azure Kubernetes Serv: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is a container platform and plays no part in Azure Files identity-based authentication. What AD DS needs is identities synced to Microsoft Entra ID.
780be327c533.You must place your file share in the sa: An Azure file share lives in a storage account, not in an on-premises subnet. Clients only need network line of sight to a domain controller and the share, not co-location.
780be327c533.You must disable SMB encryption on the s: SMB encryption has no relationship to AD DS authentication, and Microsoft recommends keeping it on. Disabling it is not a requirement and would weaken security.

0b4d52d3bca3.You can configure multiple identity sour: The identity source is set at the storage account level, not per file share. All shares in the account use the same identity source, so you cannot mix sources share by share.
0b4d52d3bca3.You can configure one identity source pe: Identity sources are configured per storage account, not per subscription. Different storage accounts in the same subscription can use different identity sources.
0b4d52d3bca3.Identity sources are not configurable; a: Identity-based authentication is configurable and is the recommended alternative to account keys. You choose one of the supported identity sources per storage account.

e87832145f1c.NFS: Network File System (NFS) shares in Azure Files do not support Kerberos identity-based authentication; they rely on network-level security such as private endpoints or service endpoints instead.
e87832145f1c.FTP: Azure Files does not support File Transfer Protocol (FTP). File shares are accessed over SMB, NFS, or the REST API, and Kerberos identity-based authentication applies to SMB.
e87832145f1c.SFTP: SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) is a feature of Azure Blob Storage, not Azure Files. Azure Files identity-based authentication with Kerberos works over SMB.

af0d2dfe4e89.Access is granted because Kerberos uses: Kerberos delegation does not bypass authorization. Even with a valid ticket, Azure Files checks share-level role assignments and NTFS permissions and refuses access if they are missing.
af0d2dfe4e89.The storage account automatically genera: Azure Files never creates temporary keys for users who lack permission. An unauthorized identity simply receives an access denied error.
af0d2dfe4e89.Azure Files automatically downgrades to: Azure Files SMB shares do not support anonymous access, so there is no fallback. A user without the required permissions is denied.

bf1471b9ab3f.On‑premises Active Directory Domain Serv: On-premises AD DS requires identities that exist in an on-premises domain and are synced to Microsoft Entra ID. Cloud-only accounts are not in AD DS, so this source does not fit.
bf1471b9ab3f.Microsoft Entra Kerberos: Microsoft Entra Kerberos started out for hybrid identities synced from on-premises AD DS. It now also supports cloud-only users on Entra-joined Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025 clients, but the marked answer reflects the long-established choice, Entra Domain Services.
bf1471b9ab3f.Google Workspace: Google Workspace is not an identity source supported by Azure Files. Kerberos authentication for file shares comes only from AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services, or Microsoft Entra Kerberos.

00d3a7430a1a.Only Microsoft Entra Domain Services: Microsoft Entra Domain Services is a managed domain, not the option built for synced hybrid identities without domain controllers. Saying only Entra Domain Services ignores Microsoft Entra Kerberos.
00d3a7430a1a.Only on‑premises Active Directory Domain: On-premises AD DS works with hybrid users but requires line of sight to domain controllers. Saying only AD DS ignores Microsoft Entra Kerberos, which serves hybrid identities directly from Entra ID.
00d3a7430a1a.None of the above: This blanket option is wrong because Microsoft Entra Kerberos does support hybrid identities synced to Microsoft Entra ID, so at least one listed choice is correct.

9dac0057881c.Storage account keys rotate automaticall: Storage account keys do not rotate automatically every hour. They change only when you rotate them manually or through a Key Vault or policy-driven process.
9dac0057881c.Kerberos authentication is slower than u: Speed is not the reason to avoid sharing account keys, and this claim misframes the comparison. The concern is security: one key grants full access to everything in the account.
9dac0057881c.Using keys disables storage account encr: Using account keys does not turn off encryption at rest. Storage encryption is always on, whatever authentication method clients use.

fa9766c4c4ed.No lock: With no lock, a user with the right role can read, modify, and also delete the resource. Nothing prevents deletion, so it does not meet the requirement.
fa9766c4c4ed.ReadOnly lock: A ReadOnly lock blocks both modification and deletion. The question needs users to still modify the resource, which ReadOnly does not allow.
fa9766c4c4ed.Contributor lock: Contributor is an Azure role-based access control (RBAC) role, not a lock type. Azure resource locks come in only two levels: CanNotDelete and ReadOnly.

d9ae54247dbb.CanNotDelete lock: A CanNotDelete lock only blocks deletion; users can still modify the resource. It does not limit them to read-only operations.
d9ae54247dbb.Modify lock: Modify is not an Azure lock level. Resource locks come only as CanNotDelete and ReadOnly.
d9ae54247dbb.No lock: Without a lock, users with the right permissions can modify and delete the resource freely. That is the opposite of restricting them to reads.

95d08c01ab20.Locks at a parent scope apply only to th: Locks are inherited. A lock on a subscription or resource group applies to every resource inside it, including resources created later.
95d08c01ab20.Locks at a resource level override locks: A lower-level lock cannot loosen a parent lock. All applicable locks combine, and the most restrictive one wins.
95d08c01ab20.Locks only apply to subscriptions and no: Locks can be applied at the subscription, resource group, or individual resource level. They are not limited to subscriptions.

f3a10c3f9778.Control‑plane operations (such as updati: Control-plane operations, such as updating a resource's properties, are exactly what locks restrict. A ReadOnly lock blocks such updates.
f3a10c3f9778.Deleting resources: Deleting resources is what locks are designed to prevent. Both CanNotDelete and ReadOnly locks block deletion.
f3a10c3f9778.Listing keys for a storage account: Listing storage account keys is a control-plane POST operation, and a ReadOnly lock blocks it. So locks do affect this operation.

2adc2df96b4d.Reading blob data from a container: Reading blob data is a data-plane operation, which resource locks do not restrict. A ReadOnly lock on the account still lets authorized clients read blobs.
2adc2df96b4d.Uploading a file via SMB: Uploading through SMB is a data-plane operation on Azure Files. Locks restrict control-plane management actions, so the upload itself is not prevented.
2adc2df96b4d.Connecting to the storage account using: Authenticating with Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) credentials and accessing data is data-plane activity. A ReadOnly lock does not block it.

59ac701a62d8.The resource can be deleted but cannot b: Neither lock allows deletion, and the resource's own ReadOnly lock blocks changes too. Combined, deletion stays blocked, so the resource cannot be deleted.
59ac701a62d8.The resource can be modified but cannot: This describes CanNotDelete alone. The resource also has a ReadOnly lock, and since the most restrictive lock applies, modifications are blocked as well.
59ac701a62d8.Neither lock applies because they confli: Locks do not cancel each other out. When multiple locks apply, they combine and the most restrictive one takes effect.

1566673837e9.It does not affect role assignment; RBAC: Role assignments are control-plane operations handled by Azure Resource Manager, not data-plane operations. A ReadOnly lock therefore blocks creating them at that scope.
1566673837e9.It automatically grants Owner role to th: Locks never grant roles. Creating a lock needs permissions you already hold and assigns nothing to anyone.
Locks never change their own level. A ReadOnly lock stays ReadOnly until someone with permission edits or removes it.

5241b2f562d8.ReadOnly lock: A ReadOnly lock blocks modifications as well as deletion. The requirement is to keep allowing changes, so ReadOnly is too restrictive.
5241b2f562d8.No lock: Without a lock, nothing stops deletion beyond role permissions. It does not meet the goal of preventing deletion.
5241b2f562d8.DenyAction lock: DenyAction is not a resource lock level; locks are only CanNotDelete or ReadOnly. DenyAction is an Azure Policy effect, a separate feature.

aa5e173ee7f2.Locks apply only to specific resource ty: Resource locks are not tied to particular resource types. They can be applied to any Azure resource, and at resource group and subscription scope as well.
Locks and Azure Policy are separate controls that both apply. A lock does not override or disable policy definitions.
aa5e173ee7f2.Locks are ignored by users with Owner ro: Locks apply to everyone, including Owners. An Owner can remove a lock, but while it exists their delete or change operations are blocked.

7ea3f2abd3f7.SSPR is enabled by default for all users: SSPR for regular users is not on by default; an administrator must enable it for selected users or all users. Only administrator accounts have a separate SSPR policy enabled by default.
7ea3f2abd3f7.SSPR requires no licensing and can be us: Full self-service password reset for cloud users needs at least Microsoft Entra ID P1 or an equivalent Microsoft 365 license. The free tier only allows users to change a known password.
7ea3f2abd3f7.SSPR requires a Global Administrator rol: Global Administrator is not the only role that can enable SSPR. The less privileged Authentication Policy Administrator role can configure SSPR settings.

8a9ebf5c9ee7.User Administrator: User Administrator manages users and groups and can reset some passwords. It is not the role that configures the tenant's SSPR policy.
8a9ebf5c9ee7.Helpdesk Administrator: Helpdesk Administrator can reset passwords for some non-admin users. It cannot enable or configure SSPR for groups.
8a9ebf5c9ee7.Security Reader: Security Reader has read-only access to security information. It cannot change any configuration, including SSPR settings.

775d9d87f069.Microsoft Entra ID Free tier: The Microsoft Entra ID Free tier lets cloud users change a known password but does not include self-service password reset for them. At least P1 is required.
775d9d87f069.Microsoft Entra ID P2: Microsoft Entra ID P2 includes SSPR and MFA, but it is more than needed. The minimum license that covers these features is P1.
775d9d87f069.Microsoft 365 Business Standard: Microsoft 365 Business Standard does not include Microsoft Entra ID P1, so it does not provide the full SSPR and MFA feature set the question asks about. Business Premium includes P1.

e15d7b1639d8.All users in the tenant automatically ge: Choosing selected users limits SSPR to members of the chosen group. Enabling it for everyone requires the All setting instead.
e15d7b1639d8.Users must be assigned the Global Admini: End users do not need any administrator role to use SSPR. Being in the targeted group and registering authentication methods is enough.
e15d7b1639d8.SSPR will only reset expired passwords,: SSPR handles both resetting forgotten passwords and unlocking locked accounts. It is not limited to expired passwords.

aa31c7a2c76a.It eliminates the need for multi‑factor: SSPR does not remove the need for MFA. It actually uses multiple verification methods so users prove who they are before resetting a password.
aa31c7a2c76a.It automatically assigns passwords to us: SSPR lets users pick their own new password after verifying their identity. It does not generate or assign passwords for them.
aa31c7a2c76a.It prevents users from changing their pa: This is the opposite of what SSPR does. Its whole purpose is to let users change or reset passwords without involving the help desk.

5f3af57f263b.Social media login and password hint: Social media logins and password hints are not SSPR verification methods. SSPR uses methods such as email, phone call, text message, the Microsoft Authenticator app, and security questions.
5f3af57f263b.Fingerprint scan and iris scan: Fingerprint and iris scans are not offered as SSPR verification methods. Users verify with configured methods such as email, phone, text message, or the authenticator app.
5f3af57f263b.Security questions and geolocation: Security questions are an SSPR option, but geolocation is not a verification method. So this pair is not a valid combination of SSPR methods.

9afdc34d7ddc.A usage location for each user: A usage location is needed for assigning some licenses, not for SSPR registration. It does not make users register their authentication methods.
9afdc34d7ddc.A group policy object in Active Director: An on-premises Group Policy Object does not control registration for Microsoft Entra ID SSPR. Registration requirements are set in the SSPR settings in the Entra admin center.
9afdc34d7ddc.Custom domain names for password reset e: Custom domain names do not affect whether users register authentication methods. SSPR registration is driven by the registration settings, not domains.

e32017815a43.You cannot enable SSPR for all users at: You can enable SSPR for all users at once by choosing the All option. Piloting is a best practice, not a technical requirement.
e32017815a43.SSPR only works for users in a single gr: SSPR is not limited to a single group in general; it can be enabled for all users. Selecting one group is just how the pilot option is scoped.
e32017815a43.SSPR requires per‑user licensing that mu: Licensing is not the reason to pilot. SSPR comes with Microsoft Entra ID P1 and other licenses, and a pilot is about validating configuration and user experience.

b53031eff83c.Owner: Owner grants full access to manage all resources and to assign roles. It is the most privileged built-in role, the opposite of read-only.
b53031eff83c.Contributor: Contributor can create, update, and delete all resources. It allows changes, so it is not a read-only role.
b53031eff83c.User Access Administrator: User Access Administrator manages role assignments, which changes who has access. It is not a read-only view of resources.

ae8ab0c53dc9.Owner: Owner allows full resource management but also allows assigning roles. The question excludes role assignment, so Owner grants too much.
ae8ab0c53dc9.Reader: Reader only allows viewing resources. It cannot manage or change anything, so it does not meet the full-management requirement.
ae8ab0c53dc9.Guest Inviter: Guest Inviter is a Microsoft Entra ID directory role for inviting external guests, not an Azure resource role. It grants no rights to manage Azure resources.

244bf31d0210.Contributor: Contributor can manage all resources but cannot assign roles. The question needs both full management and role assignment.
244bf31d0210.User Access Administrator: User Access Administrator can assign roles but cannot manage resources themselves. It does not give full management access.
244bf31d0210.Reader: Reader can only view resources. It cannot change resources or assign roles.

3c2306442279.Reader: Reader can view resources and role assignments but cannot change who has access. It does not let the user manage access permissions.
3c2306442279.Contributor: Contributor manages resources but explicitly cannot assign roles. It is the reverse of what the scenario needs.
3c2306442279.Owner: Owner can manage access but also has full control of resources. The scenario says the user should not have full control, so Owner grants too much.

4473a8904243.Contributor: Contributor can create, change, and delete resources. It goes far beyond viewing, so it is not least privilege here.
4473a8904243.Owner: Owner is the most privileged built-in role, with full control and role assignment rights. It is the opposite of view-only.
4473a8904243.Tag Contributor: Tag Contributor lets a user change tags on resources, which is an action. It is not a general view-only role.

09d2a1f27e93.Reader: Reader can view tags but cannot add or change them. It does not meet the requirement to assign tags.
09d2a1f27e93.Contributor: Contributor can manage tags but also grants full management of the resources. The question asks to avoid giving those broader permissions.
09d2a1f27e93.Owner: Owner grants full control plus role assignment. That is far more than needed for managing tags.

6ec39da37e76.Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/write: Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/write relates to managing the subscription resource itself. It does not grant the right to create role assignments.
6ec39da37e76.Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/read: Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/read only lets you read storage account properties. It has nothing to do with assigning roles.
6ec39da37e76.Microsoft.Security/accessPolicies/read: This is not the action that controls role assignments; it belongs to a different resource provider. Assigning roles requires Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write.

c9b46b998c3d.The Azure subscription ID: A subscription ID identifies one possible scope, but it does not by itself set where a role applies. The scope you choose (management group, subscription, resource group, or resource) does.
c9b46b998c3d.The user's email domain: A user's email domain has no effect on where a role assignment applies. Scope is chosen from the Azure resource hierarchy.
c9b46b998c3d.The storage account tier: A storage account's performance or access tier is unrelated to role assignments. The selected scope determines where permissions apply.

Picking the role first risks assigning it at the wrong level. Microsoft's guidance is to identify the scope first, then choose the role at that scope.
Order matters because the scope sets where permissions apply. Starting from the scope helps avoid granting access more broadly than intended.
c21416470828.Assign the role at the subscription leve: Assigning at subscription level does apply to everything below it, but that grants more access than may be needed. It is not a recommended order of steps.

2875121af402.Management group: A management group can contain many subscriptions. Assigning there would give access far beyond the one resource group required.
2875121af402.Subscription: Assigning at the subscription would give access to every resource group in it. The requirement is to limit access to a single resource group.
2875121af402.Individual resource: Assigning at a single resource would cover only that resource. The user needs to manage all resources in the resource group.

c233202703b7.A role assignment at a resource group do: Azure role-based access control (RBAC) assignments at a resource group flow down to every resource inside it, so this statement is the exact opposite of how inheritance works.
c233202703b7.Role assignments override resource locks: Role assignments and resource locks are separate controls; a lock such as CanNotDelete blocks the operation even for an Owner, so role assignments never override locks.
c233202703b7.Role assignments apply only to specific: Role assignments are scoped to management groups, subscriptions, resource groups or resources, not to resource providers, and they inherit downward to child scopes regardless of provider.

06cc846a29b6.The ability to assign roles at the manag: Contributor cannot assign roles at any scope, and a subscription-level assignment never grants rights at the parent management group, because inheritance only flows downward to child scopes.
06cc846a29b6.Read‑only access to all resources: Read-only access is what the Reader role provides; Contributor goes much further by allowing create, update and delete of all resources in the subscription.
06cc846a29b6.The ability to grant administrative acce: Contributor is an Azure resource role and grants no Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) directory roles or tenant-level administrative rights; those are managed separately through Entra roles.

45e21ee2615a.Only during the creation of a resource: Azure Policy evaluates resources on more than creation: updates, new or changed policy assignments, definition updates and the periodic compliance scan all trigger evaluation too.
45e21ee2615a.When a user logs in to the portal: Signing in to the Azure portal is an identity event handled by Microsoft Entra ID and does not cause Azure Policy to evaluate any resources.
45e21ee2615a.Only when a resource is deleted: Deleting a resource does not trigger a compliance evaluation; Azure Policy evaluates resources when they are created or updated, when assignments or definitions change, and during periodic scans.

3dc8b0b40b59.Audit: Audit does not deny anything; it lets the request complete and records a warning event in the Activity Log while marking the resource non-compliant.
3dc8b0b40b59.Modify: Modify changes resource properties or tags during a create or update request to bring it into compliance, rather than blocking the request outright.
3dc8b0b40b59.DeployIfNotExists: DeployIfNotExists deploys a related resource or configuration through a template when it is missing; it does not deny the triggering request.

2f5d8987cc38.Deny: Deny blocks the create or update request entirely, so the non-compliant operation never completes, which is the opposite of what this scenario describes.
2f5d8987cc38.Modify: Modify actively changes properties or tags on the resource during the request to make it compliant; it does not simply allow and record a non-compliant state.
2f5d8987cc38.DenyAction: DenyAction blocks specific actions on a resource, currently delete requests, so it prevents the operation rather than letting it complete and logging it.

00b1ec06a04f.To deny a resource creation if it doesn': Denying a non-compliant create or update is the job of the Deny effect; Modify instead changes the request so the resource becomes compliant.
00b1ec06a04f.To log non‑compliant resources without t: Recording non-compliance without any action describes the Audit effect, whereas Modify actively alters properties such as tags to enforce compliance.
00b1ec06a04f.To deploy related resources alongside th: Deploying related resources alongside the evaluated one is what DeployIfNotExists does; Modify only changes properties of the resource being created or updated.

34acab9b76d1.It denies any resource creation that doe: Denying non-compliant resource creation is the Deny effect; DeployIfNotExists lets the request proceed and then deploys a missing related resource or setting.
34acab9b76d1.It automatically deletes the non‑complia: No Azure Policy effect deletes resources; DeployIfNotExists remediates by deploying additional configuration through an Azure Resource Manager template, not by removing anything.
34acab9b76d1.It generates an alert but does not modif: Flagging without changing anything is closer to Audit or AuditIfNotExists; DeployIfNotExists actually deploys a resource or configuration to bring the environment into compliance.

d664b61757a2.Deny blocks the resource creation while: DenyAction does not merely log; it actively blocks the targeted action, such as a delete request, while Deny blocks non-compliant create or update requests.
d664b61757a2.DenyAction is deprecated and replaced by: DenyAction is a current, supported effect introduced relatively recently, not a deprecated one; it complements Deny rather than being replaced by it.
d664b61757a2.DenyAction is less restrictive than Audi: Audit blocks nothing and only records non-compliance, so DenyAction, which actually blocks requests, is more restrictive than Audit, not less.

412e9139fd9d.Audit effects have no impact on complian: Audit effects do affect compliance: they mark resources non-compliant in Azure Policy compliance results, and they are not a metrics feed for Azure Monitor.
412e9139fd9d.Audit effects automatically fix non‑comp: Audit effects only report non-compliance and never change resources; automatic remediation comes from Modify or DeployIfNotExists with remediation tasks.
412e9139fd9d.Audit effects are required by law before: No law requires auditing before enforcement; starting with Audit is a best practice to gauge impact and avoid disrupting workloads when Deny is later applied.

c11a5b752b9e.A single policy definition applied to a: A single policy definition assigned to a scope is just a policy assignment; an initiative bundles many definitions together into one set.
c11a5b752b9e.A built‑in role that grants policy manag: Policy management permissions come from roles such as Resource Policy Contributor; an initiative is a collection of policy definitions, not a role.
c11a5b752b9e.A property that instructs Azure to ignor: Skipping evaluation is handled by exclusions or exemptions; an initiative is a group of policy definitions assigned together, not a setting that ignores evaluation.

4133e6224615.Azure Policy determines who can perform: This reverses the two services: RBAC decides who can perform actions, while Azure Policy evaluates resource properties regardless of who makes the request.
4133e6224615.Azure Policy is used only to assign role: Azure Policy does not assign roles, and RBAC does not judge resource properties; role assignments belong to RBAC and compliance enforcement belongs to Azure Policy.
4133e6224615.Azure Policy and RBAC are the same and a: Azure Policy and RBAC are distinct services with different purposes, one governing resource properties and the other governing user permissions, so they cannot be used interchangeably.

cef2fdd1e034.Assign policies first, then assign roles: In this question's framing, roles should be granted first so users can act, and policies are then layered on to ensure those actions produce compliant resources.
cef2fdd1e034.Order does not matter because they opera: Although Azure Policy and RBAC are evaluated independently, the question expects a recommended sequence of granting access with roles and then enforcing compliance with policies.
cef2fdd1e034.Assign roles and policies concurrently i: Role assignments and policy assignments are separate objects created through separate operations; there is no single combined assignment that sets both at once.

d2ee6c72e52b.It allows the resource deployment but ma: Allowing the operation while flagging non-compliance describes the Audit effect; DenyAction actively blocks the targeted request.
d2ee6c72e52b.It removes the need for role assignments: DenyAction does not replace role assignments; users still need RBAC permissions to act, and DenyAction adds a block on top of what RBAC allows.
d2ee6c72e52b.It deploys a remediation script to fix t: Deploying remediation is the role of DeployIfNotExists or Modify; DenyAction only blocks requests and never deploys scripts or fixes resources.

1db4fe8f9095.Initiatives are required to enable autom: Remediation tasks work with individual Modify or DeployIfNotExists policy assignments too, so an initiative is not a prerequisite for automatic remediation.
1db4fe8f9095.Initiatives reduce the cost of policy en: Azure Policy itself has no per-policy charge for Azure resources, so grouping policies into an initiative is about manageability and reporting, not lowering cost.
1db4fe8f9095.Initiatives allow you to bypass policy e: Initiatives do not bypass evaluation; every policy in the set is still evaluated, and bypassing would require exclusions or exemptions instead.

60ff17f1d633.Name: The rule name is just a unique label for identification within the network security group (NSG); it has no influence on the order in which rules are processed.
60ff17f1d633.Direction: Direction decides whether a rule applies to inbound or outbound traffic, but within each direction the priority number sets the evaluation order.
60ff17f1d633.Protocol: Protocol specifies TCP, UDP, ICMP or Any for matching traffic; it is a match condition, not the property that controls evaluation order.

379d3daa16d4.Allow the traffic: NSGs follow a deny-by-default model: traffic not matched by an allow rule hits the DenyAllInbound or DenyAllOutBound default rule and is denied.
379d3daa16d4.Forward the traffic to a firewall: NSGs do not forward traffic anywhere; sending traffic to a firewall requires a user-defined route, while unmatched NSG traffic is simply denied.
379d3daa16d4.Drop the traffic and log to Azure Monito: Unmatched traffic is denied, but NSGs do not automatically send logs to Azure Monitor; logging requires configuring flow logs separately.

Next hop is a property of routes in a route table, not of NSG rules; NSG rules filter traffic and never decide where packets are routed.
10f8d264386b.It indicates whether the rule applies to: Choosing TCP or UDP is the protocol property of an NSG rule; direction only distinguishes inbound from outbound traffic.
10f8d264386b.It determines the service tag used in th: Service tags are set in the source or destination fields of a rule; direction is independent and only states inbound or outbound.

58d52f412419.A reference to another NSG: NSG rules cannot reference another NSG as a source or destination; a service tag stands for Microsoft-managed IP address prefixes of a service.
58d52f412419.A custom DNS name for the rule: Service tags are not DNS names; they are Microsoft-managed labels such as Storage or AzureLoadBalancer that represent sets of IP prefixes.

2c591d130d49.They are deleted automatically when you: Default rules are created automatically with every new NSG, not deleted; they always exist and can only be overridden by custom rules.

f113c3eaea46.AllowInternetInBound: No default AllowInternetInBound rule exists; inbound internet traffic is denied by default, and probes use the AzureLoadBalancer tag instead.

DenyAllInbound applies to inbound traffic; outbound traffic is handled by the separate DenyAllOutBound default rule.

06c29878eb2c.DenyAllOutBound: DenyAllOutBound blocks outbound traffic not matched by an earlier rule, so it is the opposite of allowing internet traffic.
06c29878eb2c.AllowAzureLoadBalancerOutBound: There is no default outbound rule named AllowAzureLoadBalancerOutBound; the load balancer default rule exists only for inbound traffic.

3e07486ef242.It allows outbound traffic only to Azure: DenyAllOutBound allows nothing; outbound traffic to Azure services is permitted by other rules, such as AllowInternetOutBound or custom service tag rules.
Inbound traffic is blocked by the separate DenyAllInbound rule; DenyAllOutBound applies only to outbound traffic.
Internet-bound traffic is allowed by the AllowInternetOutBound rule; DenyAllOutBound is the final rule that blocks everything else.

566dbe122298.NSGs apply only to inbound traffic, not: NSGs filter both inbound and outbound traffic, each with its own rules and default rules, so this is not a limitation.

074b2f582184.They are an extension of Azure Firewall: Security admin rules are part of Azure Virtual Network Manager, not Azure Firewall, and they work alongside NSGs rather than replacing them.

2eb05fb0bdd7.The process of connecting an on‑premises: Connecting an on-premises network over VPN uses a VPN gateway and site-to-site connection, not virtual network peering, which links Azure virtual networks.
2eb05fb0bdd7.An alternative to network security group: Peering provides connectivity, not traffic filtering, so it is not an alternative to network security groups, which are still needed to control traffic.
2eb05fb0bdd7.A method for extending a virtual network: Peering does work across subscriptions, but it links two separate virtual networks; it does not extend one network, and nothing happens by default without creating it.

3b70515576cc.Traffic between Azure services and on‑pr: Traffic to on-premises networks requires a VPN or ExpressRoute connection; peering only connects Azure virtual networks to each other.
3b70515576cc.Traffic to Azure DNS servers only: Peering is not limited to Azure DNS traffic; all traffic between the peered virtual networks travels over the Microsoft backbone.

245db1626593.It uses an ExpressRoute gateway for conn: Peering does not use an ExpressRoute gateway; it connects virtual networks directly over the Microsoft backbone without any gateway.
Peering needs no VPN gateway; gateways are used for a separate VNet-to-VNet option that sends traffic through encrypted IPsec tunnels instead of direct backbone peering.

460ebbda2e65.It is used when connecting VNets in the: Same-region connections are local virtual network peering; global peering connects virtual networks in different Azure regions.
460ebbda2e65.It allows transitive routing between VNe: Global peering, like local peering, is non-transitive; routing through a hub requires a network virtual appliance or gateway with user-defined routes.
460ebbda2e65.It doesn't support resource communicatio: Global peering supports virtual networks in different subscriptions and even different Microsoft Entra tenants, so this restriction is false.

cada0e082c78.Up to 10 peerings: 10 peerings is far below the real limit; a virtual network supports up to 500 peerings by default.
cada0e082c78.Up to 100 peerings: 100 peerings understates the limit; the default is 500 peerings per virtual network, rising to 1000 with Azure Virtual Network Manager.
cada0e082c78.Unlimited peerings: Peerings are not unlimited; the default is 500 per virtual network, and Azure Virtual Network Manager raises it to 1000.

bf5aa2933abf.Connecting VNets across subscriptions in: Peering supports virtual networks in different subscriptions within the same tenant, and even across tenants, so no gateway is needed.
bf5aa2933abf.Using user‑defined routes (UDRs) within: User-defined routes (UDRs) within a single virtual network work through route tables and need no virtual network gateway.

33a8fc021e32.It allows the peered VNet to use the gat: Using remote gateways is for cross-premises connectivity through a VPN or ExpressRoute gateway, not for general internet-bound traffic.
33a8fc021e32.It requires both VNets to have their own: Only the remote virtual network needs a gateway; the virtual network using remote gateways must not have its own gateway.
33a8fc021e32.It automatically enables transitive rout: Using remote gateways does not make peering transitive between virtual networks; it only lets the peered network share the remote gateway for cross-premises traffic.

9a44e9016990.It allows transitive connectivity betwee: Service chaining does not make peering transitive; it uses user-defined routes to send traffic through an appliance, which is a different mechanism.
9a44e9016990.It is automatically enabled when you cre: Service chaining is not automatic; you must create user-defined routes pointing to the network virtual appliance in the peered network.
9a44e9016990.It can only be done between VNets in dif: Service chaining works in the same tenant or across tenants; it is not restricted to virtual networks in different tenants.

fd5729c83f53.No limitation; basic load balancer funct: There is a limitation: resources in a globally peered network cannot reach a Basic Load Balancer's frontend IP, which is a key reason to use the Standard SKU.
fd5729c83f53.You can only have one backend pool behin: No such backend pool rule exists; the real issue is that Basic Load Balancer frontends are not reachable across global peering.
fd5729c83f53.Global peering requires you to use a VPN: Global peering does not require a VPN gateway; the limitation is only that Basic Load Balancer frontends cannot be reached across it, which the Standard SKU solves.

cebd3346cd28.You cannot modify the address space of a: Address space of a peered virtual network can be modified; prefixes can be added or removed while the peering remains in place.
cebd3346cd28.You must remove the peering before modif: Removing the peering is no longer necessary; you can modify the address space and then sync the peering.
cebd3346cd28.You can only reduce the address space, n: Both expanding and reducing are supported; prefixes can be added or removed on a peered virtual network.

30188be6f0d9.Routing to on‑premises networks via a VP: Routing to on-premises through a VPN gateway is a supported use of the virtual network gateway next hop, for example forced tunneling.

30188be6f0d9.Routing to the internet: Sending internet-bound traffic to a VPN gateway, known as forced tunneling, is a supported use of a virtual network gateway as next hop.

8f57f3c07b32.Address prefix: Address prefix defines the destination range a route matches; it does not attach the route table to a subnet.
8f57f3c07b32.Next hop type: Next hop type defines where matching traffic is sent, such as a virtual appliance, but does not attach the route table to a subnet.
8f57f3c07b32.Metric: Azure user-defined routes have no metric property; route selection uses longest prefix match, and attaching a table requires a subnet association.

27cb83344d6d.System routes apply only to outbound tra: Route tables apply to outbound traffic from the subnet for both system and user-defined routes; no inbound-only versus outbound-only split exists.
27cb83344d6d.UDRs are deprecated in favor of service: User-defined routes are not deprecated; service endpoints serve a different purpose, optimizing access to Azure platform services.

e0807b7a1e53.Up to 100: 100 understates the real limit; a route table supports up to 400 routes, or 1000 with Azure Virtual Network Manager.
e0807b7a1e53.Up to 2000: 2000 exceeds the real limit; route tables support 400 routes by default and 1000 with Azure Virtual Network Manager.
